query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a gradient, self-healing thermally adaptive surface coating on CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys will induce the in-situ formation and regeneration of a lubricious tribofilm during sliding, thereby maintaining low friction and wear rates consistently from room temperature up to 800 °C under varying loads and oxidative conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a coarse-grained microstructure and no surface modifications.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply a gradient, self-healing surface coating (for example, an adaptive oxide or ceramic layer) on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests performed over the full temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C), under variable normal loads, and in an environment that permits oxidation (i.e., ambient or controlled oxidative conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: The engineered gradient coating that, upon exposure to friction and temperature, forms a continuously regenerating lubricious tribofilm.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding contact, the thermally adaptive coating reacts to the frictional heat and mechanical stress by developing a nanocrystalline glaze layer (or similar lubricious phase) that lowers interfacial shear strength. At lower temperatures, the gradient structure minimizes wear via barrier effects, while at higher temperatures the self-healing character sustains a protective lubricious film, mitigating adhesive and oxidative wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the uncoated CoCrFeNi alloy, the coated samples will exhibit a statistically lower steady-state friction coefficient and reduced specific wear rate throughout the temperature range up to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The starting CoCrFeNi alloy typically shows variability in friction performance with increased wear due to limitations in sustaining a stable lubricious surface film without tailored surface modifications.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective in conditions ranging from room temperature to 800 °C under moderate to high sliding loads in oxidative environments; its performance in non-oxidative atmospheres or under extreme load scenarios remains to be verified.
generation.uncertainty: The exact chemical composition, gradient profile, and process parameters of the coating required to optimize performance across the entire temperature and load range are not yet determined and may require fine-tuning.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of CoCrFeNi alloy specimens: one group receives the gradient, self-healing surface coating and the other group remains uncoated. Perform systematic sliding wear tests over temperatures from room temperature to 800 °C, applying a range of normal loads in an oxidative environment. Use controlled conditions to simulate real sliding contacts and record the progression of friction coefficients and wear rates.
measurements: Surface morphology and tribofilm integrity (using microscopy and spectroscopic techniques such as SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the uncoated control across the full temperature range, or if the tribofilm does not exhibit self-healing characteristics (as evidenced by degradation or discontinuity under high-temperature sliding), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

Sliding contact experiments were performed on an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy bulk specimen, with an average initial grain size of approximately 42 µm, that was fabricated by laser 3D printing of gas atomized powder. These experiments were performed in UHV (~10–9 torr) to mitigate the impact of oxidation and adsorbates. By comparison to previous literature, we show that environment can have a significant and detrimental impact on the friction and wear properties of this alloy. Representative sliding cycle-average friction coefficients are shown in Fig. 1A for two contact loads, 10 mN and 100 mN, for highly smooth, ruby spheres (Al2O3, with initial RMS surface roughness ~ 10 nm) sliding on the samples. In the low friction case, the experiments were paused mid-way for 24 hours to help elucidate the role of microstructural evolution on interface strength, and thus friction coefficient; this is discussed in more detail, below. Average steady-state friction coefficients of μss≅0.32 and μss≅0.68 were measured at 10 and 100 mN, respectively. The H13 steel exhibits a maximum friction coefficient and wear loss after 800 °C/60 min high temperature friction and wear treatment. Compared to the H13 steel, all HEA coatings exhibit smaller friction coefficient and wear loss. A minimum friction coefficient and wear loss (only 12% of H13 steel wear loss) occurs in the AlCoCrFeNiWx with the addition of 0.5 at.% W.
